text: Good evening, everybody. Welcome to our regular Council meeting of Tuesday, July 13, 2021. Call to order. As always, we are pleased to be here today on the traditional territory of Treaty 6. text: What is yours. Perfect. Thank you, Your Worship. Good evening everyone. I'm Emily Sankster, I'm a long range planner and the project lead for the age friendly strategy strategy has been in progress since late last summer, and I'm here this evening to give an overview of the process and to provide an opportunity for questions or comments that you might have before considering the recommendation to adopt the strategy. Specifically, I'll give some background on the rationale for the strategy, provide an overview of our framework and the process for developing it and summarize the vision goals needs and priority actions before we have time for discussion. So a few words on the rationale. This was an action item in our 2019 municipal development plan, and it aligns with other directional plans and policies including our social master plan, and our affordable housing strategy that's in progress. It also supports direction from the regional growth plan to plan for all communities in the region to develop as complete communities, which means that they meet residents daily needs by providing convenient access to a wide range of housing and transportation services, local services, jobs and community infrastructure. The growth plan also adopts the World Health Organization's definition of age friendly communities, which was used for this project, and which I'll describe a bit more in a moment. There are many recognized benefits of age friendly planning, and those include improved resident health and community engagement, more business opportunities and wiser use of public resources in service provision. In particular, the advantages of having a more inclusive and accessible community are not limited to older people, but can also extend to children, young families, people with disabilities, people on lower incomes and more. So the World Health Organization's framework which we used for this project for age friendly communities was first launched in 2006, and since then it's been adopted by communities worldwide. It's been endorsed by the Public Health Agency of Canada and Alberta Health, and they've produced complimentary resources to support communities planning for age friendliness. The framework, as you may have seen from the report has eight community dimensions that highlight the really wide range of things that affect health and well being for older people. Some of them address kind of quote unquote hard physical infrastructure such as public spaces and housing. Others address quote unquote soft but really no less important infrastructure such as community programs, communication frameworks and support services. So Beaumont's age friendly strategy assess needs and recommended priority actions under each of the eight dimensions. So just a word on our process as well. The strategy was developed in two general stages, the first of which focused on understanding local needs under each community dimension. And the second that focused on developing a strategy to address those needs. We started in summer 2020 with project and engagement planning, and one of our first tasks was to establish a working group of about a dozen members to guide the project. We comprised representatives from various city departments, as well as from the 50 plus club village regional housing foundation, the primary care network, the library drive happiness cycling without age, and some members at large as well. Based on meetings with our working group, and on public and stakeholder engagement in the fall. We developed a working draft document that identified key needs under each dimension. It was reviewed and validated by the working group, and was then brought to SLT and committee of the whole for information and view. After that, the project team sought additional working group input. We did further external research conducted some additional interviews and discussions with relevant city departments to determine feasibility and coordinate with existing programs and initiatives. In the summer, we fleshed out the working draft in early 2021 to incorporate actions to address the needs and to incorporate an implementation plan. We brought the draft document back to the working group and other internal reviewers, including SLT for comment and refinement at that point. We then held a final draft for a second round of public engagement in May, seeking residents thoughts on how effective they thought the actions would be, as well as any other comments that they might have on the strategy. Overall, the actions received generally positive rankings of about three or four out of five, and comments from the survey provided a variety of specific suggestions for city programs but didn't flag new needs that hadn't previously been considered. We maintained the overall content of the strategy, made a few minor revisions for clarification and emphasis as needed, and the revised strategy is what we're presenting here this evening. So our key needs and actions. The overall vision and goals of the strategy, as mentioned, were developed in collaboration with the working group and presented to the public for feedback last fall. Our vision is of Beaumont as an age-friendly city, where the well-being and full inclusion of older people supports an accessible, healthy and vibrant community for everyone. So again, the focus is on older adults, but this can have benefits for the community as a whole. The goals set out are more specific aspirations and priorities as they apply to those eight community dimensions that I noted before. I won't go through each need identified under all these dimensions, but I will note that they are wide ranging, as we anticipated by the breadth of the World Health Organization framework. They encompassed everything from infrastructure and facilities to programs and services, whether those are managed and influenced by the city or by a range of private government and community entities. In developing a strategy, the working group and the project team aim to identify at least one action to respond to each identified need, recognizing that some actions can address more than one need, and that can potentially be under more than one dimension. So that's why some actions appear under several dimensions in Section 4 of the document, even if they only appear once in the implementation plan in Section 5. For example, developing a more extensive and easy to find web page with resources of interest to older people can help address needs related to social participation, but also communication and information and community supports and health services. So it appears in three places. We also included two actions to recognize that many positive things are already in place in the city of Beaumont, and it would be very difficult for this strategy to predict and include every possible opportunity to make the city more age friendly. So these actions that we've included are number one, to maintain and improve upon our existing community strengths, and number two, to adopt an age friendly perspective throughout city planning operations and other initiatives. So these are there to allow for flexibility to seize opportunities as they're identified or as they arise. Also, because this is a city strategy, the actions focus on what the city's role is, even if other community partners may be involved. This plan doesn't contain actions that the city will be able to evaluate but not able to influence. For instance, recognizing that much of the legislation and many of the requirements that apply to businesses are provincial, the recommendations in the strategy focus on reviewing the city's own design guidelines and developing resources to support local businesses in becoming more accessible. And finally, administration recognizes that the plan contains 25 priority actions, which is a fairly large number. This is partly due to the number of community dimensions and the diversity of needs to be considered and addressed. It's also because, as you can see from the implementation plan, many of the actions involve relatively straightforward short term initiatives or tweaks to ongoing programs that might be considered quote unquote low hanging fruit. So should the age friendly strategy be adopted this evening, administration is looking forward to continuing to work with community partners to put the strategy into practice. Age friendly planning relies on multi sectoral partnerships and on communication. And many members of our project working group have expressed interest in continuing to be involved in implementation and evaluation. We expect that progress reporting will take place every one to two years, led by long range planning and FCSS. And so with that, I will thank you for very much for your attention and invite any questions or comments regarding the process, the strategy or the potential implementation.
